diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the narrow sheath-hidden head
diagnostic_checks.check: A perennial usually 50–100 cm, with ~5–10 cm narrow, spikelike panicle partly enclosed in an inflated flag sheath. The true ligule is usually a TINY hair fringe only 0.2–0.3 mm.

diagnostic_checks.look: Check fine lemma hair and the one-flowered spikelet

diagnostic_checks.look: Record the pericarp response but don't force a false ID

diagnostic_checks.certainty: Detailed UT analysis, not a standalone field test

diagnostic_checks.look: Look INSIDE upper leaf sheaths for very short flowering heads
diagnostic_checks.check: Poverty dropseed is an ANNUAL with ~1–4 cm narrow terminal and AXILLARY panicles, frequently enclosed or partly enclosed by upper leaf sheaths. A seed-bearing plant can appear headless from a distant photo.
diagnostic_checks.compare: S. compositus and S. clandestinus are tall perennials with more substantial generally 5–26 cm panicles; winter surviving dry sheaths aren't proof of life cycle.

diagnostic_checks.look: Open one single-flowered spikelet, not a bunch of grass awns

diagnostic_checks.compare: S. clandestinus has bigger 5–7 mm spikelets and hairy opaque mature lemmas; the difference requires actual scale.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase typical morphology; this genus varies among varieties and closely related S. neglectus

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm a short fibrous-rooted ANNUAL base

diagnostic_checks.compare: Tall/composite dropseed perennial bases can also be dormant and brown; they are different species.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species life cycle; image of true root-to-head connection pending

head.reference: Panicles 6–30 cm with purplish or banded spikelets; head outline varies, pigmentation alone not species diagnostic.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow the narrow crowded head before counting flowers
diagnostic_checks.check: The contracted narrow lance-shaped PANICLE is typically about 8–25 cm long but only 0.6–1.5 cm wide, with 2–6 cm close-appressed branches; count complete spikelets, not bare flowering axis joints.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Purpletop Tridens flavus has very long drooping/spreading panicle branches; Buckley's Tridentopsis has much more openly spaced spreading branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase source, whole attached head photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Open a spikelet and compare the TWO near-equal glumes
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew gives 4–10 florets within 4–10 mm laterally compressed spikelets. The two glumes are about 3–4 mm and ONE-veined, nearly equal in length; fertile lemma 3–4 mm and three-veined.
diagnostic_checks.compare: T. texanus glumes usually only 2–3 mm and distinctly shorter than a 4–5 mm lemma. Narrow-headed Tridentopsis mutica has usually longer 8–13 mm spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-backed ranges; mm-scale single-plant dissection not independently verified

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect lemma NERVE HAIRS and short ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: White tridens is the relatively glabrous exception: Kew reports the lemma midvein and margins without conspicuous cilia, a very short HAIR-FRINGE ligule 0.2–0.5 mm, and short knotty rhizomes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Tridentopsis mutica has clearly pubescent lower lemma nerves and a ciliate membrane ligule. The whitish head color alone is not evidence.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Comparison is useful but 'glabrous' may require microscopy; photo pending

head.reference: Long 15–35 cm or larger drooping panicle with flexuous, often viscid branches; airy silhouette retained.

ligule.source: Kew POWO GrassBase (source under accepted or historical combination); FNA regional descriptions
ligule.reference: A ciliate membrane (not just a pure hair ring) may be visually interpreted as fringe of hairs in a photo; allow both broad visual answers pending actual leaf-junction macro.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look along an open head at bare bases of drooping branches
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes an open 15–40 cm panicle, with long branches that are often bare for roughly the lower THIRD to HALF and become conspicuously divergent or drooping; hairy branch axils and viscid/glandular branch surfaces may be present.
diagnostic_checks.compare: T. albescens branches hug a thin, narrow crowded panicle; T. texanus has a smaller, flexuous open panicle with many flowers per spikelet.

diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Tridens flavus

diagnostic_checks.look: Count florets and the three lemma nerves
diagnostic_checks.check: The FNA/GrassBase accounts give 4–8 fertile florets per 5–10 mm spikelet; one-veined lower and upper glumes and a 3–5 mm fertile THREE-veined lemma. Midvein and lateral veins can extend as very short points beyond the two-toothed lemma tip.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Triplasiella has an open head but often a smaller 2–3 mm lemma with only the midvein continuing as a point; photograph the actual three nerve tips.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-backed; needs separated mature lemma with 10–20x and same-scale lookalike

diagnostic_checks.look: Reveal the ciliate membrane beneath the collar hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA reports a tiny ciliate MEMBRANE ligule up to 0.5 mm, while Kew GrassBase calls it a hair fringe. The broad visual key permits both visible forms, NOT two different species.
diagnostic_checks.compare: T. albescens usually has a short hair-fringe-only account and close narrow head, but both need a collar macro to compare.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Source-category difference retained; no inner-collar image certified

diagnostic_checks.look: Trace the flexible branches of the shorter open panicle

diagnostic_checks.look: Check very long spaced branches with few spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: The open 10–28 cm panicle often has stiff, widely spaced spreading/ascending 4–13 cm primary branches with scattered spikelets. This is not a dense slender bottlebrush.
diagnostic_checks.compare: T. mutica has a very narrow contracted linear head, 7–20(25) cm long but only 0.3–0.8 cm across.

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the unusually LONG lower glume
diagnostic_checks.check: Its 7–10 mm spikelets usually contain 3–5 florets. LOWER glume ~5–6 mm is often slightly LONGER than upper glume ~4–5 mm, BOTH one-veined; fertile lemma 4–6 mm and three-veined.

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the ciliate membrane, then isolate a lemma

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm the exceptionally narrow compressed head
diagnostic_checks.check: The mature panicle is commonly LINEAR, 7–20(25) cm long and only 0.3–0.8 cm wide, with dense appressed spikelets; source documents a tufted perennial. Don't judge a flattened dried voucher as original branch width.

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure glumes before deciding which variety
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical 8–13 mm spikelets bear 5–11 florets. LOWER and UPPER glumes ~3–5.5 mm can vary from ONE to SEVEN veins. Historic varietal keys separate shorter one-veined var. mutica from longer 3–7-veined var. elongata; do not force a single vein cutoff on the species.

diagnostic_checks.certainty: Species-level Kew account; variety concepts require source/voucher crosswalk

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect hairy lower lemma nerves and short ciliate membrane
diagnostic_checks.check: Mature fertile lemma ~3.5–5.5 mm, three-veined, hairy below on the midvein and margins; apex entire to shallowly notched but **muticous** (= NO long lemma awn). Ligule is a ciliate MEMBRANE ~0.5–1 mm, not merely an unspecified hair ring.

diagnostic_checks.certainty: Accepted-name/old-synonym source-backed; field membrane may look hair-fringed

field_rule:
Supplemental field cue (Peterson and colleagues, Taxon 65, 2016) — Check the entire open panicle from its base to its tip. The published diagnosis gives 10–30 cm long and 8–20 cm wide.

Start with real source-verified Triplasiella panicles in panels 0–1, fresh Texas flowering heads in panel 5, mature reddish spikelets in panel 6 and pale fresh branching spikelets in panel 11. Panels 8–9 show the plant among other low vegetation, but the underground rootstock is obscured and neighbors may be different grasses. The stiff bristly head BEHIND panel 1 belongs to another grass; its warning arrow must remain. Open branches are a first clue, not a confirmed ID: verify t

broad_group_note: Group-level broad head and habit screened. Current accepted name crosswalk is supported by Kew, but a species-specific morphological description under Triplasiella/Tridens/Tridentopsis is still needed. Not marked externally verified.

head.reference: Triplasiella separated from Triplasis by wide, open panicles 10–30 cm long and 8–20 cm wide, palea keels smooth/scabrous and absence of cleistogamous spikelets in upper sheaths. Correct accepted name vs historical Tridens eragrostoides is explicitly documented.

ligule.source: Peterson et al. 2016 Triplasiella diagnosis plus regional older Tridens eragrostoides ligule descriptions
ligule.reference: Historic sources document membranous true ligule under older Tridens eragrostoides; current hair-only state was unsafe; keep both broad visual answers, photo microscopy pending. Do not assert genus-level 2016 diagnosis alone certifies ligule type.

taxonomy.source: Kew POWO accepted Triplasiella eragrostoides; Peterson et al. (2016) new genus
taxonomy.reference: Accepted: Triplasiella eragrostoides. Historical Tridens eragrostoides and Tridentopsis eragrostoides are homotypic synonyms; not separate species. Distinct from true Triplasis by smooth/scabrous palea keels and absence of upper-sheath cleistogamous spikelets.

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the complete wide, open flowering head
diagnostic_checks.check: Peterson et al. (2016) defines the genus with a broad 10–30 cm long by 8–20 cm wide open panicle, much wider than true Triplasis species (usually 1–7 x 1–6 cm). This is a first sorting clue, not standalone ID.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Tridens flavus also forms open panicles; compare actual mature lemmas and nerve tips, not overall silhouette.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Peer-reviewed 2016 genus diagnosis; exact photos not yet anatomy-certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2016 — Triplasiella genus diagnosis

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare BOTH palea keels and a mature lemma nerve tip
diagnostic_checks.check: Triplasiella has PALEA KEELS that are smooth or scabrous, NOT densely ciliate like Triplasis; a regional grass key describes a typically 2–3 mm lemma with MIDNERVE extending slightly as a point, while Tridens flavus usually 3–5 mm with midvein and both lateral nerves tending to project.
diagnostic_checks.compare: The key's old Tridentopsis eragrostoides name is a SYNONYM of Triplasiella, not a separate species. Compare an attached mature floret from the same plant.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Peer-reviewed genus-level distinction plus regional comparison; lemma dimensions concept dependent
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2016 — Triplasiella vs Triplasis

diagnostic_checks.look: Search upper leaf sheaths but do not invent hidden flowers
diagnostic_checks.check: Triplasiella differs from true Triplasis in NOT producing CLEISTOGAMOUS spikelets concealed in upper leaf sheaths. The prior FNA/range treatments have described a membranous ligule while older broad categories sometimes emphasize hairs. Keep both visual collar states until a sharp same-plant macro.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Triplasis commonly bears upper-sheath hidden flowers and densely HAIRY palea keels; look at the actual sheath and 2-keeled palea, not neighboring plants in a background photo.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: 2016 genus concept and modern accepted-name Kew crosswalk; absence must be assessed on real specimen
diagnostic_checks.source: Peterson et al. 2016; accepted name in Kew POWO

diagnostic_review.note: Botanical source comparisons checked, not yet verified against same-plant local dissections, exact gallery photo role, or BONAP NAPA county nativity.

head.source: Kew POWO GrassBase under Brachiaria fasciculata, https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:1156554-2/general-information
head.reference: 3–20 unilateral racemes along a central axis; sometimes secondary branches; one-sided state supported.

habit.reference: Annual decumbent culms rooting from lower nodes; surface-running mat possible.

diagnostic_checks.look: Study the short clasping lower glume
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew GrassBase under Brachiaria fasciculata describes paired obovate spikelets about 2.4–3 mm, with a LOWER glume only about one-quarter to one-third of their length, usually FIVE-veined.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas signalgrass has nearly twice-as-long spikelets and a much larger lower glume; creeping signalgrass has an even shorter often veinless lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew synonym-based source; taxon-concept crosswalk retained

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for secondary branchlets on the one-sided rays
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually 3–20 primary unilateral racemes (1–8 cm), sometimes with SECONDARY side branches, plus an irregular distribution of paired spikelets. Hair-fringe true ligule ~1 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Creeping signalgrass's 5–15 shorter 1–4 cm branches usually have crowded regularly paired spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase source checked; actual head photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the annual runner and upper lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Low annual stems may root at lower nodes, producing a mat. The upper fertile lemma is indurated with a transversely rugose surface. Pubescent nodes and tubercle-based leaf hairs may be present.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Paspalum forms a different spikelet with lower glume usually absent; U. reptans has shorter spikelets and a truncate tiny lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew taxon-linked morphology; specimen-level check remains pending

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

head.source: Kew POWO GrassBase under Brachiaria reptans, https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:426280-1/general-information

habit.reference: Annual decumbent stems root at lower nodes; may form surface mats.

ligule.reference: Hair-fringe ligule, not an obvious free papery flap.

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the minute translucent lower glume

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the crowded spikelet pairs and hairy pedicels
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually 5–15 closely spaced unilateral racemes, each 1–4 cm, with two-rowed crowded PAIRS along three-angled rachis and fine hairs on the pedicels. Hair-fringe true ligule.
diagnostic_checks.compare: U. fusca can have secondary branching and a looser panicle; Paspalum usually lacks the developed lower glume.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and Flora Zambesiaca; attached macro needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the creeping node and mature fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Annual trailing stems root at lower nodes. The hardened fertile upper lemma is finely wrinkled and ends in a tiny point (mucronate), rather than a conspicuous long projecting awn.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Other signalgrasses share that lemma surface; use spikelet length and lower-glume proportion together.

field_rule: Identify endangered Texas wild-rice from legally permitted observation only: ribbon leaves streaming in running water, emerge a flowering axis, follow top ascending female-bearing and lower spreading male-bearing floral regions with dangling anthers. Final uncertain identifications belong to authorized botanical specialists. Do not touch/enter/collect protected plants.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

head.reference: Flowering stalk holds lower hanging male flowers and upper erect female flowers; Hays County San Marcos River endemic. Do not touch or collect protected plants.

habit.reference: Rooted under running water, leaves stream parallel to current; stolons permit clonal spread. Do not require an exposed underground rhizome to match a field observation. Published GrassBase account calls it annual under some conditions; TPWD/USFWS emphasize perennial aquatic behavior.

awns.reference: Pistillate/female spikelets have slender awns 9–35 mm; male spikelets lack this feature, so observable awn state depends on sex and reproductive stage.

protected_observation.source: Texas Parks and Wildlife official endangered species profile
protected_observation.reference: Only upper two miles San Marcos River, Hays County; federally/state endangered. Observe without touching, entering protected habitat, cutting or collecting. Lower dangling staminate branches vs upper upright pistillate branches.

diagnostic_checks.look: Observe ONLY: lower dangling MALE versus upper upright FEMALE branches
diagnostic_checks.check: Endangered Texas wild-rice has a 16–31 cm emergent flowering stalk with lower side branches of PENDULOUS male spikelets, and upper stiffly ASCENDING female spikelets. Females bear slender ~9–35 mm awns; males lack those long awns. Do not touch, enter habitat, or collect protected plants.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant cutgrass also has both sexes in its panicle but male and female are borne along the SAME branch, with the females nearer the tips.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Texas Parks and Wildlife verified morphology; NO manipulation or collection is permitted for this key

diagnostic_checks.look: Identify an aquatic rooted ribbon-leaf habit from a lawful viewpoint
diagnostic_checks.check: In cool clear fast-flowing upper San Marcos River water, long ribbonlike blades STREAM WITH THE CURRENT and have a prominent central vein; flowering culms may emerge while rooted vegetative shoots stay submerged. This is a perennial by TPWD, though older global GrassBase calls it annual in one description.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant cutgrass usually has stout reedlike culms and leaves emergent ABOVE shallow swamp water, and a far larger airy head.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: TPWD and USFWS ecology and accepted range; no field access or habitat disturbance for data collection

diagnostic_checks.look: Know the one-flowered GLUMELESS male/female spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: Both sexes bear one-flowered spikelets with glumes ABSENT. Male units (often ~7–9 mm) are awnless with stamens; female (~6.5–12.5 mm) have a long awned lemma and develop slender cylindrical grains. The true ligule is a membrane 5–15 mm in GrassBase.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant cutgrass also has glumeless unisexual spikelets, but females' awns are much shorter (~2–3 mm) and floral sexes occur on the same flowering branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Kew and TPWD; floral anatomy for training from legally sourced existing verified images, not collecting protected plants

diagnostic_review.note: Source-linked botanical comparisons complete for first checklist pass only; photo parts, exact lineage where relevant and Hays field specimens not certified. Endangered Zizania strictly observe without disturbance.

head.source: Diggs et al. Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded p.262
head.reference: Large 30–60 cm loose wetland panicle with male and female spikelets intermixed (Diggs et al., uploaded p.262), in contrast to Texas wild-rice's lower male/upper female branching arrangement. Retain airy option for gross outline.

habit.reference: Strong rhizomatous wetland perennial, often 1.5–3 m.

sex_branch.source: Kew GrassBase Zizaniopsis miliacea; TPWD Texas wild-rice comparison
sex_branch.reference: Male and female spikelets share the SAME panicle branch, male basal and female more distal. This differs from Zizania texana lower all-male branches and upper all-female branches.

diagnostic_checks.look: Follow ONE branch to see both floral sexes
diagnostic_checks.check: Giant cutgrass is MONOECIOUS, with male and female single-flowered spikelets on the SAME main panicle BRANCHES; Kew describes male below female on each such mixed-sex branch. The open panicle is very large, ~30–60 cm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice separates sexes on different branches of the head: lower dangling male branches and higher upright female branches.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase and TPWD both document same-branch sex arrangement; branch-sex photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure a blunt female floret and its very SHORT awn
diagnostic_checks.check: The glumes are both ABSENT/obscure. Male and female spikelets each carry one floret, around 6–8 mm in GrassBase; female lemma typically 7-veined with one SHORT (~2–3 mm) awn, male lemma awnless with anthers. Only the complete fertile floret confirms flower sex.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice female units carry 9–35 mm awns while male branches hang below; both species can have large panicles and glumeless spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew species source checked; same-flower scale and sex detail currently needs fine diagnostic photos

diagnostic_checks.look: Check emergent rhizomatous canes, sawn blade edges and big ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: Giant cutgrass is an erect, perennial 2–3 m wetland cane from elongated rhizomes. Leaf margins are minutely SAW-TOOTHED (serrulate), and the true inner ligule is a large ECILIATE 6–20 mm MEMBRANE, much longer than Phragmites' tiny ciliate membrane.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Texas wild-rice has long current-streaming mostly submerged leaves and is restricted to the upper San Marcos; do not use broad wetland occurrence as endemic species evidence.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew/GrassBase and TPWD contrast; connected rhizome, blade edge and 6–20 mm ligule actual photo pending

diagnostic_review.note: Source-linked botanical comparisons complete for first checklist pass only; photo parts, exact lineage where relevant and Hays field specimens not certified. Endangered Zizania strictly observe without disturbance.
